lesson_title: One Ferry, Three Bakeries, Fourteen Takeaways
hook_text: One lagoon, one town, one street — and you already shop in all four market structures every week.
clip_script: A holiday town sits across a lagoon, and one company runs the only ferry. Ride, or drive ninety minutes around. Push the fare up and most people sigh and tap their cards — that's a price maker, and its only leash is the demand curve. Inland, three bakeries feed a farming town. Raise your bread price alone? Rivals hold still and your ovens cool. Cut it? They match by Thursday and everyone's just poorer. So the price freezes for a year at a time — no handshake needed, just three bakers playing chess. The rivalry pours into fresher deliveries and sponsor boards instead. And the day the three owners share a table and murmur two rand up, all of us — that murmur is a case file, and the Competition Tribunal can take a tenth of their turnover. Back at the taxi rank, fourteen takeaways trade elbow to elbow, each one slightly its own: crispest chips, halaal counter, open till the last taxi. Each owns a tiny monopoly its regulars will pay five rand extra for — until a fat margin invites two new shops and the profit melts back to normal. One ferry, three bakeries, fourteen takeaways: monopoly, oligopoly, monopolistic competition. Same three questions every time — output at MR equals MC, price off the demand curve, verdict from average cost. Only two dials change: the slope, and the door.
visual_style: A single camera glide across one illustrated coastline: a lone ferry crossing a lagoon, then three bakery vans circling a frozen price sign, then a neon strip of fourteen takeaways; two big dials labelled SLOPE and DOOR turn between scenes.
mood: Curious and cinematic, building to a satisfying unifying reveal.
pacing: Three unhurried scene beats — ferry, bakeries, takeaways — then a rapid-fire recap over the turning dials.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to draw all four market structures from one diagram with two dials.
